title: Why Sea Otters Don't Freeze With 0 Blubber 🦦
description:
How does a sea otter stay warm in icy water with no blubber at all? Its fur is the densest of any animal, up to a million hairs per square inch, trapping air so cold water never reaches its skin, and its muscles burn energy as heat so fast it eats about a quarter of its body weight every day.

topic: The Sea Otter Paradox: how does an animal with no blubber stay warm in icy water?
script: A sea otter has no blubber, but you'd freeze long before it would. Why? Whales and seals wrap up in thick fat. The otter's secret is fur. Up to a million hairs on every square inch, the densest fur of any animal. That's more hairs on a stamp-sized patch than you have on your whole head. Those hairs trap a layer of air, so cold water never touches its skin. That's why otters groom for hours, fluffing air into their coats. But fur alone isn't enough. Its muscles leak energy as heat, like an engine idling all day. So it burns fuel about three times faster than other animals its size. To keep up, it eats about a quarter of its body weight every single day. Would you trade your jacket for a million hairs, and a quarter of your weight in snacks?
key_facts: Sea otters have no blubber, unlike whales and seals; they rely on fur (Seattle Aquarium, Marine Mammal Center)
Densest fur of any animal: up to about 1 million hairs per square inch (Seattle Aquarium); a human head has roughly 100,000 hairs
Fur traps a layer of air so water doesn't reach the skin; otters spend hours a day grooming and blowing/fluffing air into the coat
Wright et al. 2021 (Science): skeletal muscle mitochondria 'leak' energy as heat; resting metabolic rate roughly 3x that of similar-sized mammals
Eat about 25% of body weight per day (Seattle Aquarium / Marine Mammal Center)
